nameStory: The dunlin gets its name from the old English word "dunling," which means "little dun-colored one." "Dun" refers to a dull brownish-gray color, perfectly describing this sandpiper's muted plumage that helps it blend seamlessly with mudflats and beaches. The name was first recorded way back in the 1530s, making it one of our oldest bird names still in common use.
description: The dunlin is a medium-sized sandpiper about the size of a robin, with a distinctive curved black bill that droops slightly at the tip. In breeding plumage, it sports a bold black belly patch that makes it easy to identify among flocks of other sandpipers. Outside of breeding season, dunlin are much more subdued, wearing plain gray-brown upperparts and clean white underparts. These hardy shorebirds are built for probing deep into mud and sand with their sensitive, flexible bills.

idTips.label: Curved Bill
idTips.description: Look for the distinctive black bill that curves downward at the tip, longer than most similar sandpipers and perfect for probing deep into soft mud - you can often see them pushing it completely into the substrate

idTips.label: Black Belly Patch
idTips.description: In spring and early summer, adults develop a striking black patch across the lower breast and belly that stands out like a dark bib against their rufous-streaked upperparts

idTips.label: Size and Posture
idTips.description: Noticeably larger than peeps like semipalmated sandpipers, with a more hunched feeding posture as they probe methodically rather than picking at the surface

idTips.label: Flight Pattern
idTips.description: In flight, shows a thin white wing stripe and appears somewhat stocky with steady wingbeats, often flying in tight, coordinated flocks that twist and turn as one unit

idTips.label: Winter Plumage
idTips.description: Non-breeding birds are plain gray-brown above with clean white underparts, but still retain the distinctive curved bill that separates them from other gray sandpipers

idTips.label: Feeding Behavior
idTips.description: Probes deeply and systematically in soft mud, often disappearing their entire bill and sometimes even getting mud on their face - quite different from the quick pecking of smaller sandpipers

habitat: In New England, dunlin frequent mudflats, salt marshes, and sandy beaches along the coast, especially areas with soft substrate where they can probe for marine worms and small crustaceans. They're most commonly found in protected bays and estuaries during migration, often mixing with flocks of other sandpipers on extensive tidal flats. Look for them at places like Plum Island, Cape Cod Bay, and other major coastal birding spots.

seasonality.spring: Peak migration occurs from late April through May, with birds showing their striking black belly patches and rusty-streaked breeding plumage. This is the best time to see them in their most distinctive plumage before they head to Arctic breeding grounds.
seasonality.summer: Only non-breeding individuals remain in New England during summer months, appearing in plain gray-brown plumage without the distinctive black belly patch.
seasonality.fall: Migration peaks from August through October, with birds in various stages of molt from breeding to winter plumage. Juveniles appear with neat, scaled upperparts and are often more numerous than adults.
seasonality.winter: Small numbers winter along the New England coast, particularly in Massachusetts, wearing their plain gray-brown winter plumage and often associating with other wintering shorebirds.

funFact: Dunlin are incredible navigators that can fly non-stop for over 1,800 miles during migration, and some populations that nest in northern Alaska actually fly all the way to Asia to spend the winter - completely bypassing perfectly good wintering habitat along North American coasts!
confusionNotes: Dunlin are most easily confused with sanderling and other medium-sized sandpipers, but the curved bill is your best friend - remember "Dunlin = Downward curve." In winter plumage when the black belly patch is gone, that droopy bill tip is still the giveaway, along with their slightly larger size and more methodical probing behavior compared to the quick surface-picking of sanderling.
contextualKnowledge: The dunlin is sometimes called the "default sandpiper" by birders because it's so widespread and common that it serves as the standard for comparing other sandpipers. However, this abundance can be deceiving - their Arctic breeding grounds are highly vulnerable to climate change, making these familiar birds potentially less common in the future.
compareHints: Among the Calidris sandpipers, dunlin are larger than the "peeps" (semipalmated, least, and white-rumped sandpipers) but smaller than red knot, with that diagnostic curved bill that none of the others possess. Unlike the straight-billed sanderling that runs along wave edges, dunlin prefer mudflats and probe much deeper. They're chunkier than stilt sandpipers and lack the long legs, while being much more common than the rocky-shore-loving purple sandpiper.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among the Calidris sandpipers, sanderlings are notably stockier with a thicker bill than the needle-billed Least Sandpiper or Semipalmated Sandpiper.
Within the Calidris genus, Semipalmated Sandpipers are most similar to Western Sandpipers but have blunter, shorter bills and less rusty coloring in breeding plumage.
Among its Calidris cousins, the Least Sandpiper's yellow-green legs immediately set it apart from the black-legged Semipalmated and Sanderling.
Among the many Calidris sandpipers, Purple Sandpiper is unique for its consistently dark plumage and exclusive rocky habitat preference.
Among the Calidris sandpipers, White-rumped is most similar to Baird's Sandpiper, but Baird's lacks the white rump and has a more buff-colored breast.

Among the Calidris sandpipers in New England, pectoral sandpipers are distinguished by their larger size and that signature sharp breast line - dunlin have curved bills and different streaking, while the various 'peeps' (least, semipalmated) are much smaller.
Among the Calidris sandpipers, Red Knot is the second-largest and most robust, much chunkier than Sanderling or Semipalmated Sandpiper.
Among New England's Calidris sandpipers, the Stilt Sandpiper is the tallest and longest-legged, easily distinguished from the tiny 'peeps' like Least and Semipalmated Sandpipers.
Among the small Calidris sandpipers, Baird's stands out with its notably long wing projection past the tail - much longer than Semipalmated or Least Sandpipers.
Among New England's Calidris sandpipers, Buff-breasted is unique for its solid peachy-tan underparts and preference for grassy areas over mudflats.

Among New England's small sandpipers, Western Sandpipers are most easily confused with Semipalmated Sandpipers, but Westerns have longer, more drooped bill tips and often show more rusty coloring in breeding plumage.
Among Calidris sandpipers, Ruffs are unique in their extreme sexual size difference - much more pronounced than in Dunlin or Pectoral Sandpipers.
Among its Calidris sandpiper relatives, the Curlew Sandpiper's curved bill immediately sets it apart from straight-billed species like Sanderling and Semipalmated Sandpiper.
Among its Calidris relatives in New England, Little Stint is smaller than Least Sandpiper (already our tiniest regular sandpiper) and much smaller than Semipalmated Sandpiper.
Compared to other small Calidris sandpipers in New England, Red-necked Stint is smaller than Semipalmated Sandpiper and has darker legs than Least Sandpiper.
Among the Calidris sandpipers, Sharp-tailed is most similar to Pectoral Sandpiper in size and habitat preferences, but lacks the Pectoral's sharply cut breast band.
Among Calidris sandpipers, the Surfbird is uniquely stocky and rock-adapted, unlike its beach and mudflat-loving relatives.
